SINGAPORE – Singapore is launching three national artificial intelligence initiatives to combat financial crime, improve financing for smaller businesses, and enable AI agents to make transactions safely on behalf of users. Speaking at the Singapore FinTech Festival at Singapore Expo on Nov 18, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said these missions will bring together financial institutions, technology companies, researchers and public agencies to build shared capabilities in a bid to achieve more than any institution could alone. Singapore will also test promising solutions against global best practices and standards, and take those that work well towards wider deployment. To strengthen the country’s ability to detect and disrupt financial crime, Gan, who is also chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), said the Republic must connect information across the financial system while strengthening detection within each institution. “Scams are not confined within the boundary of one bank. A victim’s money can pass through several institutions within minutes. We will not be able to mitigate the risk if each institution sees only its part of the transaction chain,” he added. He noted that a proof of value is already under way with five banks, pooling transaction data securely to allow AI models to find patterns that no single bank can see on its own. title: Klarna launches AI ‘concierge’
summary: The buy now, pay later provider has waded into agentic commerce with a new tool and aims to expand its longer-term loan portfolio.
excerpt: An article from. Dive Brief. Klarna launches AI ‘concierge’. The buy now, pay later provider has waded into agentic commerce with a new tool and aims to expand its longer-term loan portfolio. Published Nov. 18, 2026. Justin Bachman Senior Reporter. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. License. Add us on Google. First published on. Dive Brief:. Klarna introduced a personal artificial intelligence assistant this week to complement its core consumer lending business, and is debuting it through waitlist invitations, the buy now, pay later company said Tuesday. “We are bringing AI and agentic commerce to the core of Klarna,” CEO Sebastian Siemiatkowski said Tuesday on a quarterly earnings call with analysts. Klarna users have spent about $34 billion since 2020 using the web browser feature in the existing app, the company said in a press release. Separately , Klarna said it’s aiming to expand its longer-term installment loans to more U. S. and European consumers. Those loans are Klarna’s fastest-growing and “highest-earning product per dollar of volume,” the company said in its earnings release. Dive Insight:. Klarna’s AI tool acts as “a personal concierge” for tasks such as booking reservations, drafting email replies, shopping and sending upcoming birthday reminders, the company said in its press release. The assistant will not complete purchases autonomously – a human is required to authorize payments, a Klarna spokesperson said. Transactions through the AI tool are through a Klarna payment method or a user’s debit card, the spokesperson said. The agent interacts via text message and is also available via Meta Platforms’ WhatsApp and Apple’s iMessage text services. The company spokesperson declined to say how many people have been invited to use the assistant so far. The Klarna tool enters a crowded field of personal AI agents, with consumer offerings that include shopping abilities from Meta’s Muse, Google’s Gemini , Instinct, OpenAI’s dots and Daydream , a New York-based online search and shopping fashion startup. ByteDance, the Beijing-based parent of social media platform TikTok outside the U. S. , also plans to release a personal AI agent, Bloomberg News reported last week. As Klarna bots begin shopping, the company is keen to grow beyond its traditional zero-interest pay later loans. That retail-based lending still accounts for about three-quarters of the company’s gross merchandise volume. Much of the growth for the lengthier “fair financing” loans has been in the U. S. , where the company has partnered with merchants such as Airbnb, Walmart and Southwest Airlines. Longer-term financing is available at 21% of Klarna’s affiliated merchants, or 283,000, up from about 150,000 a year ago, the company said. Volume for these loans has more than doubled over the past 12 months, to $12. 5 billion, compared to $6 billion in the rest of the world, Klarna said in its earnings report. The company also called out Europe as a region for growth. In the U. S. , Klarna’s longer duration loans have terms up to three years and interest rates to a maximum of 35. 99%. For these loans, Klarna targets a transaction margin of 3% to 4% of volume, or “more than three times” what the traditional pay later loans earn, the company said in its earnings report. For the third quarter, Klarna reported a net loss of $65 million , compared to a $95 million loss in the same period last year. Revenue rose 12% to $1 billion. Active users rose 7% from a year ago, to 122 million in 26 countries. Klarna also projected a profit for the last three months of 2026, citing “a good start” to the quarter. The earnings call was expected to be the last for Klarna CFO Niclas Neglen, who is leaving the company at year-end to become the chief financial officer at Adyen, the Amsterdam-based payments processor. Last week, Klarna announced that Chris Koegel, a vice president at trading platform Robinhood, will become its new CFO effective Jan. 1. Recom

title: Data silos threaten banks’ competitive edge in AI
summary: Nearly three in four consumers using AI for banking tasks opt for ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini — almost double those using a bank's chatbot, a McKinsey report found.
excerpt: An article from. Dive Brief. Data silos threaten banks’ competitive edge in AI. Nearly three in four consumers using AI for banking tasks opt for ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini — almost double those using a bank’s chatbot, a McKinsey report found. Published Nov. 18, 2026. Makenzie Holland Senior News Writer. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. License. Add us on Google. First published on. Dive Brief:. Artificial intelligence is disrupting banks’ business models, prompting a race to reap the benefits before the window of opportunity closes, according to a McKinsey & Co. report published last week. Nearly three in four consumers using AI for banking turn to OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude or Google’s Gemini for banking tasks, almost double the amount who use a bank’s chatbot, the report found. The trend highlights a quickly fading grace period, as consumers across demographics embrace AI faster than previous technology waves, according to McKinsey. As banks pour investment dollars into AI efforts, “speed could determine how much value the bank keeps, and unlike in past technology cycles, a late start may not offer chances to catch up, depending on how the profits get reinvested,” the report said. Dive Insight:. As banks seek to strike a balance between accelerating AI use and maintaining operations and security, they’re also contending with digital technology challenges. Thousands of customers from JPMorgan Chase, among other firms, reported issues accessing their online accounts Monday. While navigating traditional technology challenges, data readiness continues to be an issue for chief information officers on their AI journeys. Nearly half o f banking executives ranked data readiness as their top AI obstacle, McKinsey found. To see better results with AI projects over time, banks need to build institutional intelligence – starting with data that agents can consume at scale, according to McKinsey. Banks also need to build context, which McKinsey described as a map of customer accounts with permissions set in place, and implement an encoded judgment call policy agents can reuse. “The customer wants a capable deputy that asks for permission, and the bank that gets the permission model right may win the mandate to move the customer’s money,” the report said. Still, high-value AI deployments remain stuck in pilot purgatory, largely due to meaningful business data also being trapped inside siloed legacy systems, according to a report from information management compan y Iron Mountain. Instead of spending time scaling agents, skilled IT and data science personnel are burning hours wrangling data manually to support projects, according to 84% of IT leaders. In a move to improve analyst access to data, Northern Trust worked with Microsoft Frontier Company’s forward-deployed engineering team to launch an AI-powered onboarding agent. The agent cut data preparation time b y 83%, from 2½ weeks to three days. “Accelerating our strategic execution and the transformation of the company is AI,” Northern Trust CEO Michael O’Grady said during the bank’s third-quarter earnings call in October. “Our focus has been on converting widespread adoption into business value. ”. title: Stitch Launches Stitch AI, Bringing Agentic AI Directly Into Banking Operations
excerpt: Agentic AI for banks launches with 'Anyone can be a hero' campaign. DUBAI, UAE and RIYADH, Saudi Arabia , Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Stitch today announced the launch of Stitch AI,bringing agentic AI directly into the operating system for banks and financial institutions. Natively, built into the Stitch operating system, financial institutions can deploy agents within existing governance and approval controls. The launch is accompanied with 'Anyone can be a hero,' a campaign film which can be viewed on stitch. co/ai. Stitch AI gives financial institutions three ways to put AI to work. Continue Reading. Copilot: Bank staff ask it to fetch data, execute a task or change a configuration in plain language. It pulls data on accounts and customers, sets up products from accounts and cards to loans, including limits, pricing, fees and eligibility, and updates workflows. Stitch Agents : Ready-made AI agents handle everyday banking operations, including onboarding, credit decisioning and collections. They operate within the bank's existing workflows, permissions and rules. Agent Harness: An enterprise-grade framework that allows banks to build, configure, test and deploy their own AI agents, with permissions, approvals, guardrails and audit trails built in. All three operate within the limits the bank sets. Above them, they ask. Most AI in banking is added on top of legacy systems, where data sits in places that were never designed to work together. Legacy tools work on incomplete copies of records, with no direct access to accounts or customers. They can answer questions but cannot execute tasks, enforce approvals or operate within the controls required by regulated financial institutions. Customer data may also pass through external systems beyond the bank's direct oversight. Stitch AI is built into the operating system. Agents act on the core system itself, through the same services the bank's products already run on, with no copies of data and no separate connectors to maintain. Every agent has its own identity, scoped permissions, hard limits, maker-checker, a full audit trail, and every control a regulated institution expects. Sensitive data, including ID numbers, account numbers, phone numbers and addresses, is masked before any model sees it. Every question, action and approval is logged with the reasoning behind it, so risk and compliance teams have a complete record of what happened and who signed it off. Banks decide where Stitch AI runs and which model it uses. It deploys in-country or in a private cloud, on your model of choice, and banks can switch models without rebuilding anything while remaining in full control of their data. "Most AI projects in banks gets stuck at the proof of concept because the systems underneath can't accept them and in this regulated industry, nobody lets an agent act without an owner and an approval. Stitch solves both. We make modernising easy, and AI comes built into the operating system, under the bank's controls, from day one. " said Mohamed Oueida, CEO of Stitch. ' Anyone can be a hero ' is now available for viewing, with two new campaign films set to be unveiled later this week. About Stitch. Stitch is the AI-native operating system for modern financial institutions. Most banks run on technology that is fragmented, decades old, and only able to take AI at the edges. Stitch replaces that infrastructure with one platform spanning lending, cards, payments, wallets and more, unifying the ledgers and workflows needed to build and run financial products. Founded in 2022 and headquartered in Riyadh, Stitch serves financial institutions around the world and is backed by leading investors including Andreessen Horowitz. SOURCE Stitch. Modal title.

title: AI in UK financial services: looking beyond the numbers in the 2026 Bank of England and FCA survey
excerpt: . Find a lawyer Our capabilities Your career. Locations. Our capabilities. News. Select language:. Locations. Our capabilities. News. Select language:. 5 MIN. AI in UK financial services: looking beyond the numbers in the 2026 Bank of England and FCA survey. Nov 16 2026 On 26 October 2026, the Bank of England and the UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) published the results of their fourth survey on AI in UK financial services. The survey updates the regulators’ evidence base on how firms are using, governing and managing AI, and supports their ongoing work against the backdrop of evolving AI capabilities and adoption. Read alongside the FCA’s recent publications on AI (see our coverage here ) and the final report of the Mills Review (see our coverage here ), the results offer useful insights into the practical pressure points emerging as firms move from experimentation towards more widespread, and potentially more autonomous, deployment of AI. In this blog post, we draw out the key themes from the survey and what they may mean for firms. AI governance is widespread, but ongoing oversight is less developed. Most respondents now report having formal AI governance arrangements: 94% have firmwide AI policies, principles or standards, and 84% have centralised AI or model-risk governance fora. But the survey identifies a notable gap between implementation of pre-deployment controls and ongoing oversight. Human approval, pre-deployment review and vendor due diligence were each reported by more than 90% of respondents, while ongoing monitoring, leakage testing and periodic review or recertification were each reported by only around half. The contrast suggests that firms’ controls are more developed at the point of deployment than during subsequent use. As we noted in our recent briefing on the FCA’s good and poor practice , the FCA has identified oversight as an area where firms are still under investing; having a governance framework is only the starting point, and firms need to demonstrate effective oversight throughout an AI system’s lifecycle. This includes senior managers understanding the AI risks within their areas of responsibility. Third-party AI may be the harder governance problem. Third-party implementations now account for 53% of reported high-materiality AI systems (up from 35% in 2024). At the same time, firms reported less direct understanding of high-materiality third-party systems than internally developed systems, relying instead mainly on vendor assurance and contractual arrangements. Oversight of third-party AI was also the most commonly reported area of governance uncertainty or implementation challenge, particularly in relation to concerns about information security and/or operational resilience. For firms, the practical challenge is to maintain effective oversight when their understanding of a system depends heavily on information supplied by a provider. Agentic AI is already here, but delegation remains limited. Although 80% of respondents reported having deployed AI agents (with a further 14% reporting plans to deploy them over the next 12 months), deployment remains largely assistive: 80% reported agents providing decision support, while only 2% reported agents with broad autonomy. Firms remain cautious about allowing agents to take consequential actions such as approving or declining customer outcomes, executing trades or placing orders, initiating, executing or blocking payments, or changing limits, thresholds and controls. The distinction between assistance and delegation is important. As we discussed in our briefing on the Mills Review final report , the regulatory risk increases as AI systems move from supporting human action to taking action themselves. Moving from AI that supports human decisions to AI that takes action itself raises additional questions about accountability, consumer protection and redress. title: Hong Kong Pushes Banks to Use AI Agents to Detect Crypto-Related Financial Crime
excerpt: Hong Kong Pushes Banks to Use AI Agents to Detect Crypto-Related Financial Crime. Hong Kong's HKMA is encouraging banks to deploy AI agents to trace crypto transactions and identify suspicious activity before funds disappear. Ethan Collins. min read. 18 November 2026. Smaller Default Bigger. Hong Kong’s monetary regulator is stepping up efforts to bring artificial intelligence into banks’ anti-money laundering systems, as stablecoins and other digital assets complicate the tracking of suspicious financial transactions. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) is exploring how AI agents could connect blockchain activity with customer information to identify potential financial crime before funds can be moved beyond recovery. Raymond Chan, the HKMA’s executive director for enforcement and anti-money laundering, said Tuesday that the regulator is working to accelerate AI adoption across the banking sector. The proposed systems could help investigators identify suspicious transaction patterns and establish links between digital wallets and real-world identities. Illicit Crypto Activity Reached $154 Billion in 2025. Chan pointed to research from blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, which estimated that illicit cryptocurrency addresses received at least $154 billion in 2025. That represented a 162% increase from the previous year, with activity involving sanctioned entities accounting for much of the rise. Stablecoins represented 84% of the reported illicit transaction value. However, Chainalysis estimated that illicit activity accounted for less than 1% of the cryptocurrency transaction volume covered by its analysis. Although blockchain transactions can be traced, determining the individuals or organizations controlling specific wallets remains a more difficult task. Chan identified the speed of connecting wallet activity to real-world identities as a central obstacle to preventing criminal proceeds from being transferred or dispersed. AI Agents Could Connect Blockchain and Customer Records. The HKMA is examining whether AI agents can help banks analyze blockchain transactions alongside customer records. These systems could identify patterns that may indicate attempts to obscure the origin of funds, including rapid transfers between cryptocurrencies and conventional currencies. Chan also said identity-related tools designed to help establish wallet ownership are being tested. The regulator has supported banks through technical assistance and workshops as financial institutions explore ways to introduce AI into their operations. A report released Tuesday by the Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research described one bank using generative AI to investigate potential money laundering. The system examined transaction records, images and customers’ digital activity. The bank reported improvements in investigation speed and accuracy, although the report did not provide specific performance figures. Most Surveyed Financial Institutions Are Adopting Generative AI. The report found that 90% of surveyed financial institutions had already adopted generative AI or planned to introduce it. For business applications, 13% had implemented AI agents, while another 56% said they planned to do so. The survey was conducted between January and March and included 39 financial institutions and eight technology providers. Despite growing adoption, participating banks identified security risks and difficulties explaining decisions made by AI systems as important concerns. Human Oversight Remains Important in Financial Crime Investigations. Abdul Rafay Gadit , co-founder of ZIG Finance, recommended that banks evaluate AI agents using historical fraud cases and operate them alongside existing monitoring systems before granting them independent authority. ("Propel" or the "Company") ( PRL ), the fintech facilitating access to credit for underserved consumers, today announced a significant advancement to its proprietary AI underwriting platform with the official launch of its enhanced cash-flow underwriting model. Built entirely in-house, the new model analyzes six months of bank transaction history in seconds to assess creditworthiness with greater precision, providing a more complete picture of a consumer's financial circumstances, beyond traditional credit bureau data. The technology allows Propel and its Bank Partner to identify creditworthy consumers who may be overlooked by conventional underwriting methods, expanding access to credit while maintaining its existing risk standards. The model launched in late Q3 2026, where initial results have demonstrated the ability to approve more consumers at the same risk thresholds. Propel estimates the new technology could expand access to credit by up to 15%, with expansion into the United States expected in early 2027. To support the launch, Propel has partnered with Plaid , a leading consumer-permissioned financial data network that connects thousands of financial institutions and fintechs. Plaid's insights into cash flow, income patterns, and financial obligations help Propel's proprietary AI models make more informed credit decisions. Propel is a leader in AI-powered non-prime underwriting, having launched its first proprietary AI model in 2015. Since then, Propel and its Bank Partners have underwritten more than two million loans and lines of credit, building a substantial proprietary dataset in a segment of the credit market that is particularly complex to underwrite. "A credit score doesn't always tell the full story of someone's financial circumstances, and that limits access to credit for millions of consumers," said Dr. Jonathan Goler, Co-Founder and Chief Risk Officer of Propel. "By combining open banking data, supported by Plaid, with sophisticated time series deep learning models, we can better understand a consumer's current financial circumstances and identify patterns that are genuinely predictive of repayment. Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) has released an AI-powered cybersecurity tool designed to help businesses identify potential vulnerabilities earlier in software development. Called CodeCheck, the free, open-source tool was developed by CBA’s security engineers and is based on an AI capability used within the bank’s software development process. The public version allows other businesses to apply a similar approach when reviewing their own code. The tool draws on CBA’s experience securing a technology environment containing approximately 2. 5 billion lines of code maintained by thousands of engineers. It works with OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code to analyse software, investigate potential security weaknesses, and provide evidence for engineers to review. CommBank Chief Security Officer Nicola Nicol said the bank developed the capability to strengthen its internal security practices before making it publicly available. “We’ve built this capability to help strengthen our own defences,” Nicol said. The release follows warnings from the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) about the speed at which attackers exploit software vulnerabilities. According to the agency’s 2025–26 Annual Cyber Threat Report, some vulnerabilities have been exploited within 48 hours of a patch or mitigation advisory being released. How CodeCheck identifies vulnerabilities. CodeCheck uses an AI harness that guides coding agents through a structured security review. It can examine individual code changes, files, or entire codebases, allowing developers to identify potential vulnerabilities during software development. Businesses can provide additional information about how their applications operate, including their intended functions and expected behaviour. The service supports linking multiple bank cards, enabling AI agents to complete shopping payments upon user authorization, thereby extending ChatGPT’s capabilities from task execution to commercial transactions. OpenAI is further extending ChatGPT’s capabilities into the realms of payments and commercial transactions. The company introduced ChatGPT Wallet, allowing its Dots AI agents to access user-linked credit cards and, upon authorization, complete product purchases and payments on behalf of users. This signifies that the role of AI agents is evolving beyond assisting with product searches and planning to encompass actual transaction execution. S. -issued credit cards to the wallet, review transaction details, and authorize payments after the AI agent has completed product selection and order preparation. The newly launched wallet supports eligible bank cards issued by American Express, Chase, MasterCard, and Visa. OpenAI processes transactions using a payment tokenization mechanism, ensuring that merchants do not directly receive users' full physical credit card information. Users’ existing credit card account relationships and associated benefits remain intact. From AI Assistant to Transaction Executor. Before payment, users must verify information such as the merchant, product, quantity, total transaction amount, payment card, and delivery or recurring payment terms, and then click to approve. Subsequently, users must complete verification via biometric methods such as Face ID or Touch ID before the agent can proceed to submit the order. This means that ChatGPT Wallet is not merely adding a bank card payment entry point to the chat interface, but rather integrating product discovery, order preparation, and payment execution into the AI agent’s workflow. title: Schwab, LPL, and Fidelity veterans launch AI firm for wealth executives
excerpt: . Schwab, LPL, and Fidelity veterans launch AI firm for wealth executives. Bridge Operating Partners debuts with deep industry pedigree and a proprietary AI system designed to sharpen decision-making for wealth firm executives. NOV 18, 2026. By Steve Randall. Former C-suite leaders from the industry's biggest platforms are betting their combined experience builds a smarter operating system for growing RIAs and family offices. The executives who built some of the largest wealth management operations in the United States have joined forces to take on the gap between a firm's growth ambitions and its capacity to execute on them. Bridge Operating Partners, launched in Scottsdale, Arizona, pairs veteran C-suite advisors with a proprietary artificial intelligence platform built to give wealth management and family office leaders sharper, faster executive decision-making. The firm's founding team carries credentials that few new entrants in the advisory technology space can match. A team built inside the industry's biggest firms. Eddie Brown, founder and chief executive officer of Bridge Operating Partners, spent years as managing director and head of Schwab Advisor Family Office at Charles Schwab, where he grew family office assets from $20 billion to more than $200 billion and oversaw $1. 2 trillion in assets, according to the company. He subsequently served as the first chief growth officer at Pathstone , a $180 billion platform, and held executive leadership roles at Fidelity Family Office Services and Citi Global Wealth Management. "Growth firms rarely stall because they lack vision, talent or market opportunity. They stall because of execution," Brown said. "I've been in their seat. I sought a better way to serve the leaders I worked with, and it led me to build the system I wish I'd had when I was in their position. ". Joining Brown are three other founding partners whose collective biographies read as a cross-section of the industry's last two decades. Paul Ferguson, formerly managing director at Schwab Advisor Family Office overseeing 165 family offices representing more than $300 billion in assets, is lead author of two industry references - The Multi-Family Office of Tomorrow and Fees and Pricing for UHNW Client Services - and serves as chief strategy officer. Stephen Chien, formerly head of AI advisor solutions at LPL Financial where he led AI strategy and governance for the firm's network of 32,000 financial advisors, takes the chief product and technology officer role. Tim Ramza, former CEO of Liveoak Technologies, which was acquired by DocuSign, and former chief innovation officer at Manulife, rounds out the founding group. What the platform actually does. Bridge's model covers three practice areas: leadership and growth, focused on helping CEOs align capital allocation and organizational design with expansion goals; firm architecture, addressing how wealth firms and family offices structure their service models and pricing; and what the firm calls sovereign AI - deploying its proprietary platform, the Bridge Operating Sovereign System, or BOSS, as an executive intelligence layer the client firm controls outright. The sovereignty framing is deliberate. Each client's command center consolidates operational reporting, tracks milestones, and surfaces decisions that need attention without sending the firm's data into a shared environment. When Bridge's engagement ends, the system stays with the firm. "Although advisors can choose from many AI tools that save them time, wealth management and family office executives do not have AI capabilities designed for leaders to help them drive strategy into execution," Chien said. "They need executive intelligence connected to their operating context, so they start each day knowing what changed, why it matters, and what decisions they need to make. ". Banking associations across Southeast Asia are advancing plans for a common approach to artificial intelligence governance and stronger cybersecurity cooperation as financial institutions accelerate their adoption of emerging technologies. The initiatives were endorsed during the 54th ASEAN Banking Council Meeting held on 13 and 14 November at the Makati Shangri-La Hotel in Manila, bringing together more than 280 banking executives, policymakers and industry experts from the region and beyond. Hosted by the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP), the meeting focused on “AI-Driven Banking in ASEAN: Securing Our Future Together. ”. Also read Marcos sees 1M Filipinos in Canada as bridge to stronger trade, security ties. Under the Committee on Cooperation in Finance, Investment, Trade and Technology, members agreed to advance work on an ASEAN-wide baseline for AI governance in banking to address differences in regulatory frameworks that could hinder cross-border deployment. The next phase of the project will develop an implementation roadmap outlining priority areas, deliverables and responsibilities. The proposed framework is intended to provide practical, principles-based guidance that ASEAN markets can adopt progressively. Regional banking associations will also strengthen information-sharing on AI-driven cyberattacks, including threats arising from the use of artificial intelligence by banks, their customers and other counterparties. The committee likewise agreed to increase regional workshops on digital scams and fraud from once to twice annually, allowing banks to exchange information on emerging threats, prevention measures and industry practices. Another initiative will examine the demand and strategic viability of tokenized deposits and stablecoins in ASEAN, particularly in relation to the Swift Ledger initiative. Meanwhile, the Committee on ASEAN Inter-Regional Relations discussed expanding cooperation through its annual study tour, with proposed topics for 2027 including green and transition finance, artificial intelligence, cross-border payments, cybersecurity, financial inclusion and data privacy. The 2027 study tour will continue to be conducted in person, with its destination to be determined through a poll among member associations. The council meeting’s outcomes underscore the regional banking industry’s push to strengthen digital resilience while developing a more coordinated approach to technological innovation and emerging financial risks. title: Digital Kiosk 3.0 brings open banking and artificial intelligence into the everyday lives of citizens
excerpt: Digital Kiosk 3. 0 brings open banking and artificial intelligence into the everyday lives of citizens. Open banking and PSD2 in Montenegro. 5637 views 0 comment(s). Digital Payment Institution module in the Digital Kiosk application: all banks and all accounts in one place, Photo: Digital Kiosk. Disclaimer: The translations are mostly done through AI translator and might not be 100% accurate. PS Promo content. 18. 11. 2026. 08:42h. What is open banking and why is it important?. Open banking allows citizens, with their explicit consent, to securely use their bank account data and initiate payments outside the application of the bank where they have an account. This concept was developed in the European Union through the PSD2 Payment Services Directive, with the aim of encouraging innovation, greater competition, and simpler use of financial services. Montenegro has adopted these rules through the Payment Transactions Law, which recognizes two key services: provision of account information and initiation of payments. These services can only be provided by licensed institutions. 2BI, the creator of the Digital Kiosk application, is licensed by the Central Bank of Montenegro to provide open banking services. Download the Digital Kiosk app for iOS or Android or scan the QR code. All banks in one place. The Digital Payment Institution module was developed based on the principles of open banking, allowing users to connect their bank accounts to the Digital Kiosk application, thus creating a universal account. Regardless of the number of banks in which they have open accounts, users receive an overview of total available funds, balances and changes on all connected accounts through a single application. The system supports accounts in all banks operating in Montenegro, so users can monitor accounts from multiple banks through one application. To link accounts, the user must have active electronic or mobile banking from their bank, through which they provide the necessary consent for data access. For the first time, citizens can have a single overview of their finances, without having to use multiple banking apps to check balances and transactions. Paying bills without overwriting data. With the new generation of the application, Digital Kiosk 3. 0, artificial intelligence becomes an integral part of everyday financial management. A digital payment institution enables simple bill payments directly from the user's bank account, without manual data entry and without the need to copy information from payment slips. Three ways to pay your bill are available to users. You can pay your bill by scanning a QR code, downloading it electronically from supported issuers, or using AI Payments, a new functionality based on artificial intelligence. It is enough to take a photo of the receipt, select an image from the phone's gallery, or upload a document from the device (a receipt received via Viber or email can be opened directly in the Digital Kiosk application), and the application automatically recognizes the data from the receipt and prepares the payment order. Instead of manually entering account numbers, call numbers and amounts, the user receives a ready-made order that he simply confirms via his bank's electronic or mobile banking. The result is a significantly faster and simpler payment that takes just a few seconds, without going to the counter, without filling out an order, and without using payment cards. Security under user control. One of the key principles of the open banking model is complete user control over their data. The user chooses which bank they want to connect to the application, which data they give access to and which payments they want to make. Access to data and confirmation of payment orders are carried out exclusively through electronic or mobile banking of the bank with which the user has an account, with their explicit consent. The Digital Kiosk cannot perform any transaction without user approval and confirmation

title: ASEAN banks map regional AI governance framework
excerpt: Text size. Save. ASEAN banking associations will develop a regional baseline for artificial intelligence governance and strengthen cooperation against AI-driven cyberattacks, scams and fraud, following the 54th ASEAN Banking Council meeting in Makati City. The council endorsed the next phase of a project to identify priority areas for a common approach to AI governance across the region’s banking markets, with the aim of addressing differences in national rules that could hamper the cross-border deployment of AI by banks. The next phase will produce an implementation roadmap outlining deliverables, sequencing and responsibilities, aligned with the ASEAN Working Group on AI Governance. The meeting, held on 13 and 14 November and hosted by the Bankers Association of the Philippines, gathered more than 280 banking executives, policymakers and experts from the 10 ASEAN countries and other markets. Beyond governance standards, members also agreed to strengthen cooperation in defending against AI-driven cyberattacks. Under the Committee on Cooperation in Finance, Investment, Trade and Technology, they will share practices addressing risks arising from banks’ use of AI, as well as its deployment by customers and other counterparties. The committee will also study demand for and the viability of tokenized deposits and stablecoins in ASEAN, particularly in relation to the Swift Ledger initiative. On digital fraud, regional banking associations will double information-sharing workshops to twice a year from once annually. Members also agreed to maintain coordination with regulators, telecommunications providers, digital platforms and law enforcement agencies. The council also endorsed the ABA Academy, a digital platform for banking education and professional development developed and managed by the BAP. The platform had 63 courses from four training partners as of the meeting. Also read Megawide 9M income jumps 75% to P876M. It also backed the Scam Ready ASEAN program, which aims to strengthen financial literacy and consumer protection through localized learning modules, public-private dialogues and awareness campaigns. The Philippines’ initial implementation through the Bank Marketing Association of the Philippines will serve as a model for rollouts in other ASEAN markets. The next ASEAN Banking Council meeting and ASEAN Banking Conference are tentatively scheduled for 9 to 12 November 2027 in Singapore. Follow Daily Tribune on Google News.
